newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Only a flag unites Northern Irish Protestants.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Only a flag unites Northern Irish Protestants.

text.p: British and proud of it, Ian Paisley flies the Union Jack flag proudly over his church on a leafy avenue in the heart of Protestant east Belfast.

For 30 years the politician-preacher has stomped around Northern Ireland railing at his twin "devils" of Irish republicanism and Roman Catholicism which he sees as imports of evil into the British-ruled province.

Paisley's thunderous accusations that a confederacy of IRA guerrillas, weak-kneed British ministers and expansionist Dublin governments aims to end the island's division and push Northern Ireland into a Catholic-ruled "All Ireland" state have won him high popularity.
But new voices from surprising quarters are rattling old-guard Unionists like Paisley seeking to defend Northern Ireland's 300-year-old union with Britain.

On the Shankill Road in working-class west Belfast, the red, white and blue Union Jack revered by Protestants as a badge of British identity also hangs over the cramped offices of David Ervine's Progressive Unionist Party (PUP).
Within the "Unionist family", however, Paisley and Ervine embody the old and the new.
Ervine is a "Loyalist", a term that denotes an unswerving allegiance to the British crown. Even so, he wants to build a peaceful co-existence with the province's pro-Irish Catholic minority.
"They (Unionists) have absolutely failed to get us towards a modern society," said Ervine, who served five years in jail for transporting a guerrilla bomb. "We want a secular political society."
Balding and moustached, wearing a double-breasted suit, Ervine brings a sharp-edged confidence and fluency to a political movement personified for many years by Paisley's fire and brimstone.

His political roots are in trade union politics as much as in the Protestant struggle for survival. He sees working-class Protestants and Catholics having a political and economic affinity despite religious differences.
Gunmen waging war to safeguard their British way of life flourished in the streets around Ervine's office until they hid their arms to match a truce called by the IRA in September 1994.

The IRA -- the Irish Republican Army -- has fought a guerrilla war for almost three decades to end British rule. The Loyalists have battled just as long to maintain it. Loyalists specifically targeted Catholics in their bloody campaign.

Ervine and others helped broker the Protestant truce which has survived, against all the odds, for two years. Because of his influence with Protestant guerrilla groups, he is distrusted by Paisley and more traditional Unionists.

Bible in one hand and a ballot box in the other, Paisley has become Northern Ireland's best known Protestant abroad, although his party has just three members in the British parliament compared with nine of the more moderate Ulster Unionist Party (UUP).

Heading his own sect, the Free Presbyterians, and his own Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), Paisley is a charismatic leader to his supporters. They lap up a fierce fundamentalism and table-thumping political oratory that is unfettered by worries about hyperbole.
Ervine and his allies say Paisley and other mainstream Protestant political leaders are out of touch with grassroots feeling in the Protestant heartlands.

But the opinion polls say differently and the emergent Loyalist political parties face a Herculean -- some say impossible -- task in denting the grip of the DUP and the UUP on Protestant support before the British election due by May.
Ervine's PUP is the political wing of the Ulster Volunteer Force, one of several banned groups that killed Catholics out of sectarian hatred and to give a bloody reply to IRA attacks.

The IRA broke its ceasefire with bombs in London, so the republican guerrillas' political arm, Sinn Fein, is barred from current multi-party talks in Northern Ireland. But the PUP and the Loyalist Ulster Democratic Party (UDP), have seats at the table because the Protestant truce has held.
Paisley condemns guerrilla violence and argues that neither Loyalists nor Sinn Fein should be allowed into full talks until the rival gunmen scrap their arms to prove faith in democracy.

The PUP despises what it regards as Paisley's populism and the UUP's middle-class attitudes. Instead it espouses a left-wing stance rarely linked with Protestants whose forebears took pride in their church and in their Britishness, asking little from the state.
Ervine champions a British identity which he says does not threaten Catholics.

Indeed, his advocacy of a pluralist Northern Ireland shorn of sectarianism and his success in convincing Protestant gunmen to hold the peace has won him grudging praise from Catholics. People on the streets of Dublin, where he is well-known through media interviews, shake his hand.
Ervine speaks for Protestants who have stared into an abyss and want to pull back. "Rather than shout at the dark, we believe that it's better to light a candle," he said.
